title: Shalya takes the reins
hookLine: Karna takes command, and asks for a king to hold his reins
carry: buddhi, discernment, should hold the reins

cards: A new commander needs a driver. In the Kaurava camp, Duryodhana turns to his friend Karna and gives him the army. Karna accepts, and then he says something honest.
Arjuna has an advantage I don't, he tells Duryodhana, in effect: he has Krishna holding his reins. If I'm to face him, I need a charioteer who knows horses the way Krishna does.
And Karna names the man: Shalya, king of Madra, the uncle of the Pandava twins, who ended up fighting on the Kaurava side.

teach.b: Duryodhana goes to Shalya and asks, and Shalya is furious. In Ganguli's English, the king takes it as an insult: he, a crowned king, told to drive for Karna, who was raised in a charioteer's house.
He nearly walks out of the camp. So Duryodhana talks him round, with an old story of the gods in which the creator Brahma himself drove the chariot for Shiva. Driving, in that story, is no shame.
Shalya agrees, with one condition: he'll say whatever he likes to Karna's face. Karna accepts. Now the layer underneath.
Before the war began, the epic tells us, Shalya promised Yudhishthira that if he ever drove for Karna against Arjuna, he would wear down Karna's courage with his words. So look at the two chariots.
Arjuna's driver is Krishna, steadying him. Karna's driver is a voice in his ear, working for the other side. Hindus have an old picture for this, from the Katha Upanishad.

Know the self as the rider, it says, and the body as the chariot. The senses are the horses, the mind is the reins, and buddhi, discernment, is the charioteer. When discernment drives, the horses run true.

teach.h: I WILL SAY WHAT I LIKE
teach.b: When it doesn't, the senses bolt like wild horses.

teach.h: A PROMISE TO THE OTHER SIDE
teach.b: Many teachers read the war's chariots through that picture: Arjuna gave his reins to Krishna; Karna handed his to a driver who was never truly his.
And the picture leaves you with one old question: who is driving?

how: Hindus meet Karna's last battle through recitations and readings of the Mahabharata, retellings, regional theater and television serials; the Karna Parva, the epic's book named for him, tells this part of the war.

o: the Kaurava commander who asks for Shalya as his driver
the king of Madra who drives a chariot for a friend
the Pandava archer who has Krishna at his reins

games.q: the new commander — tap the pairs.
p: king of Madra, at the reins

s: in the Katha Upanishad, the senses are the charioteer
the senses are the horses; buddhi, discernment, is the charioteer, and the mind is the reins.

games.q: the Katha Upanishad's chariot: it's 1am and your horses, the senses, are bolting toward one more video. who should hold the reins?
o: the horses: they know what they want.
buddhi, discernment, with the mind as the reins.
whoever is loudest in your ear.
games.why: the Upanishad makes discernment the charioteer. Karna's trouble is a driver working for the other side; Arjuna's reins are with Krishna.

practice: Rest your hands on your knees, loosely, like reins held without pulling. Picture the Katha Upanishad's chariot: the senses are the horses, the mind the reins, discernment the driver.
Breathing in, notice what's pulling hardest today: your phone, a worry, someone's voice. Breathing out, let discernment take the reins back, gently, with no yanking.
If you pray, you can ask God to steady the driver; if not, just let the breath run slow and even.

wordCard.voice: Karna. The new commander of the Kauravas, who asks for a king to drive him, and gets a king who carries a promise to the other side.

orig.note: charioteer: Krishna for Arjuna, Shalya for Karna, and in the Katha Upanishad, discernment for the self.
